title: dataprep: cleaning pipeline
text: 0.1.7 cleaning pipeline consists four sequential steps: Variable deletion (varidele): drop columns whose missing fraction threshold. Observation deletion (obsedele): drop rows run consecutive missing values longer half sides. Outlier removal (condextr): point--point weighted conditional extremum; alternatives include percoutl traditional percentile removal detect_outliers IQR / MAD masks. Short-period interpolation (shorvalu): fill remaining short gaps nearby valid values. Steps 1–3 wrapped dataprep() one-call use. Every step designed around physical constraint: valid substitute missing value exists observed value within half minutes least one side.

text: dataprep provides coherent, opinionated pipeline preprocessing tabular time-series data: Variable deletion missing-value fraction (varidele). Observation deletion consecutive missing runs (obsedele). Outlier removal point--point weighted conditional extremum (condextr) percentile (percoutl). Missing-value imputation within short periods (shorvalu) linear / LOCF / NOCB / mean / median (impute_missing). Fast reshaping wide long formats (melt, dcast) SIMD + OpenMP. Time-series tools: detrending, diurnal-cycle removal, rolling statistics, lags, resampling, decomposition, drift detection, day/night season flags. Fit / transform interfaces (prep_fit, prep_transform) prevent data leakage preprocessing. heavy routines written C++ Rcpp. Since 0.1.7, many operations parallelized OpenMP vectorized AVX2 / AVX-512 hardware supports .

title: Efficient and Flexible Data Preprocessing Tools
text: cleaning pipeline organised around four sequential steps, addressing distinct failure mode high-resolution environmental data:  Variable deletion. Drop size bins whose missing fraction exceeds threshold, downstream interpolation never extrapolate far-away anchors. Observation deletion. Drop rows whose selected columns contain consecutive missing run longer half minutes sides. Every remaining point trustworthy anchor within half minutes. Conditional extremum outlier removal. single value can global maximum still legitimate, vice versa. condextr() judges candidate context.  Short-period grouping interpolation. steps 1–3, remaining NAs sit inside short gaps valid anchor within half minutes. shorvalu() interpolates within short segment .  Interpolating across long gap silently mixes two physically distinct regimes can create new outliers segment boundary. Grouping short segments keeps interpolation local. Steps 1–3 wrapped dataprep() one-call use. design reasoning documented full vignette("dataprep-philosophy"). data1 package already-aggregated seven-column version dataset; useful input cleaning pipeline.

text: Efficient flexible preprocessing tabular time-series data. heavy routines implemented C++ via 'Rcpp', optional OpenMP parallelization SIMD acceleration (AVX2 / AVX-512) supported hardware. 0.1.7 release rewrites cleaning routines C++ delivers 1.1–1146× speedup 0.1.5. 'melt()' 'dcast()' reshaping functions achieve 0.5–1187× speedup 'melt()' 2.0–639× speedup 'dcast()' relative every one seven major alternatives R Python ecosystems, every tested scale (1,000 100,000,000 rows), produce output identical 'reshape2', 'data.table', 'tidyr', 'pandas', 'polars', 'dask', 'duckdb'. Core preprocessing steps include variable deletion missing fraction, observation deletion consecutive missing runs, point--point weighted outlier removal via conditional extremum, traditional percentile-based outlier removal, linear interpolation within short time periods. package also provides fast reshaping, descriptive statistics, missing-value diagnosis, multiple imputation strategies, winsorization, several outlier detection methods (IQR, MAD, percentile), data transformation standardization, categorical encoding, duplicate removal, data validation, data quality reporting, stratified sampling. Feature-engineering helpers cover binning, high-correlation low-variance filtering, string cleaning. Time-series tools cover detrending, diurnal-cycle removal, rolling statistics, lag creation, resampling, simple decomposition, day/night season flags, log returns, drift detection, panel balancing. Fit/transform-style machine-learning interfaces prevent data leakage preprocessing. Methods based , improved : Liang, C.-S., Wu, H., Li, H.-Y., Zhang, Q., Li, Z. & , K.-B. (2020) doi:10.1016/j.scitotenv.2020.140923 . work supported National Natural Science Foundation China (. 12301674).

title: dataprep: Efficient and Flexible Data Preprocessing Tools — dataprep-package
text: package organised around four-step cleaning pipeline: Variable deletion ([varidele()]) – drop columns         whose missing fraction exceeds threshold. Observation deletion ([obsedele()]) – drop rows         consecutive missing run longer `half` minutes         sides. Outlier removal ([condextr()]) –         point--point weighted conditional extremum detection. Short-period interpolation ([shorvalu()]) –         fill remaining short gaps nearby valid anchors. Steps 1-4 wrapped [dataprep()] one-call use. design reasoning behind ordering documented `vignette("dataprep-philosophy")`. package also provides fast wide--long long--wide reshaping ([melt()], [dcast()]), full set descriptive diagnostic helpers ([descdata()], [descplot()], [percdata()], [percplot()], [na_diagnose()], [data_report()]), fit/transform-style preprocessing plans prevent data leakage ([prep_fit()], [prep_transform()]). work supported National Natural Science Foundation China (. 12301674).

title: Cast a long-format data.frame into a wide format — dcast
code: ## --- Basic usage --------------------------------------------------  long <- data.frame(   id       = rep(1:3, each = 2),   variable = rep(c("x", "y"), 3),   value    = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) ) dcast(long, id = "id", variable = "variable", value = "value") #>   id x y #> 1  1 1 2 #> 2  2 3 4 #> 3  3 5 6   ## --- Formula interface --------------------------------------------  dcast(long, formula = id ~ variable) #>   id x y #> 1  1 1 2 #> 2  2 3 4 #> 3  3 5 6   ## --- Multiple id columns ------------------------------------------  long2 <- data.frame(   year     = rep(2020:2021, each = 4),   city     = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 2, times = 2),   variable = rep(c("temp", "rain"), 4),   value    = c(15.2, 210, 14.8, 180, 16.1, 230, 15.5, 195) )  # Explicit id columns dcast(long2, id = c("year", "city"),       variable = "variable", value = "value") #>   year city temp rain #> 1 2020    A 15.2  210 #> 2 2020    B 14.8  180 #> 3 2021    A 16.1  230 #> 4 2021    B 15.5  195  # Formula form (equivalent) dcast(long2, formula = year + city ~ variable) #>   year city temp rain #> 1 2020    A 15.2  210 #> 2 2020    B 14.8  180 #> 3 2021    A 16.1  230 #> 4 2021    B 15.5  195   ## --- Fill missing cells -------------------------------------------  # (2, "y") is missing from the input; fill = 0 gives it 0. long3 <- data.frame(   id       = c(1, 1, 2),   variable = c("x", "y", "x"),   value    = c(1, 2, 3) ) dcast(long3, id = "id",       variable = "variable", value = "value",       fill = 0) #>   id x y #> 1  1 1 2 #> 2  2 3 0   ## --- Aggregate duplicate (id, variable) pairs ---------------------  # id = 1 appears twice with variable = "x"; the mean is 1.5. long4 <- data.frame(   id       = c(1, 1, 2),   variable = c("x", "x", "x"),   value    = c(1, 2, 3) ) dcast(long4, id = "id",       variable = "variable", value = "value",       fun.aggregate = mean) #>   id   x #> 1  1 1.5 #> 2  2 3.0  # sum and length work the same way dcast(long4, id = "id",       variable = "variable", value = "value",       fun.aggregate = sum) #>   id x #> 1  1 3 #> 2  2 3   ## --- Skip NA values during scatter --------------------------------  long5 <- data.frame(   id       = c(1, 1, 2, 2),   variable = c("x", "y", "x", "y"),   value    = c(1, NA, 3, 4) )  # Default: NA stays as NA dcast(long5, id = "id",       variable = "variable", value = "value") #>   id x  y #> 1  1 1 NA #> 2  2 3  4  # na.rm = TRUE: (1, "y") is skipped, cell keeps the fill value dcast(long5, id = "id",       variable = "variable", value = "value",       na.rm = TRUE, fill = -1) #>   id x  y #> 1  1 1 NA #> 2  2 3  4   ## --- Round-trip with melt() ---------------------------------------  wide <- data.frame(id = 1:3, a = c(1.5, 2.5, 3.5), b = c(4.5, 5.5, 6.5)) back <- dcast(melt(wide, id.vars = "id"),               id = "id", variable = "variable", value = "value") back[order(back$id), ] #>   id   a   b #> 1  1 1.5 4.5 #> 2  2 2.5 5.5 #> 3  3 3.5 6.5   ## --- Larger example: 1000 rows, 50 levels -------------------------  set.seed(1) n_rows   <- 1000L n_levels <- 50L long_big <- data.frame(   id       = rep(seq_len(n_rows / n_levels), each = n_levels),   variable = rep(sprintf("v%02d", seq_len(n_levels)),                  times = n_rows / n_levels),   value    = rnorm(n_rows) ) wide_big <- dcast(long_big, id = "id",                   variable = "variable", value = "value") dim(wide_big) #> [1] 20 51

C++ backend (melt_cpp) benchmarked seven major alternatives R Python ecosystems: reshape2, data.table, tidyr, pandas, polars, dask, duckdb. Every cell measured microbenchmark using adaptive times rule. Speed-relative competitor spans 0.5x 1187x. median across tested cells competitors 10.3x Ubuntu 25.10 5.7x Windows 11 Pro Workstations; mean 58.5x 44.2x, respectively. largest gaps appear wide tables (many value columns, rows); smallest gaps appear small tables initialization overhead dominates. Representative cells (medians; numbers parentheses speed-melt() relative competitor) taken Ubuntu 25.10 host: 1e6 rows, 1 id, 9 value columns —         3.68 ms vs 7.90 ms (data.table,         2.1x), 76.8 ms (tidyr, 20.9x),         642 ms (duckdb, 174x). 1e7 rows, 1 id, 9 value columns —         37.9 ms vs 372 ms (data.table,         9.8x), 1111 ms (tidyr, 29.3x),         6423 ms (duckdb, 169x). 1e3 rows, 1 id, 10000 value columns —         3.62 ms vs 9.66 ms (data.table,         2.7x), 16.3 ms (polars, 4.5x),         4292 ms (dask, 1187x). 1e3 rows, 10 id, 10000 value columns —         25.2 ms vs 59.4 ms (polars,         2.4x), 169 ms (data.table,         6.7x), 22456 ms (dask,         891x). speed-comes three design choices: Two layout paths chosen automatically.         column-major path, output column written one         contiguous memcpy input column — fastest         possible pattern. row-major path, tiles eight         rows transposed registers         _mm512_shuffle_f64x2. SIMD streaming stores. large outputs,         _mm512_stream_pd _mm256_stream_si256         write directly memory, bypassing CPU cache         avoiding cache pollution otherwise evict         useful input data. _mm_sfence() issued         end streaming region. Hugepage hint large outputs. Output vectors         larger 512 KB allocated         Rf_allocVector() hinted         madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE), kernel can back         2 MB pages. reduces first-touch page         faults 1e8-row case. custom         allocator free pool. Two fast paths small inputs used. Tiny inputs (n <= 2048, n_meas <= 64, n_id <= 8) route melt_tiny_cpp; small inputs (total <= 131072, n_meas <= 256) route melt_small_cpp. skip hugepage hinting, OpenMP setup, thread-cap detection, keeps melt() fastest engine even tables thousand rows. output identical reshape2::melt, data.table::melt, tidyr::pivot_longer, pandas.melt, polars.unpivot, dask, duckdb UNPIVOT every tested shape, within tol = 1e-12. code: ## --- Basic usage --------------------------------------------------  df <- data.frame(id = 1:5,                  category = factor(letters[1:5]),                  v1 = rnorm(5), v2 = rnorm(5))  # Automatic ID inference: `id` and `category` are non-numeric melt(df) #>    category variable      value #> 1         a       id  1.0000000 #> 2         b       id  2.0000000 #> 3         c       id  3.0000000 #> 4         d       id  4.0000000 #> 5         e       id  5.0000000 #> 6         a       v1  0.8500435 #> 7         b       v1 -0.9253130 #> 8         c       v1  0.8935812 #> 9         d       v1 -0.9410097 #> 10        e       v1  0.5389521 #> 11        a       v2 -0.1819744 #> 12        b       v2  0.8917676 #> 13        c       v2  1.3292082 #> 14        d       v2 -0.1034661 #> 15        e       v2  0.6150646  # Explicit ID columns melt(df, id.vars = c("id", "category")) #>    id category variable      value #> 1   1        a       v1  0.8500435 #> 2   2        b       v1 -0.9253130 #> 3   3        c       v1  0.8935812 #> 4   4        d       v1 -0.9410097 #> 5   5        e       v1  0.5389521 #> 6   1        a       v2 -0.1819744 #> 7   2        b       v2  0.8917676 #> 8   3        c       v2  1.3292082 #> 9   4        d       v2 -0.1034661 #> 10  5        e       v2  0.6150646  # Explicit measure columns melt(df, measure.vars = c("v1", "v2")) #>    id category variable      value #> 1   1        a       v1  0.8500435 #> 2   2        b       v1 -0.9253130 #> 3   3        c       v1  0.8935812 #> 4   4        d       v1 -0.9410097 #> 5   5        e       v1  0.5389521 #> 6   1        a       v2 -0.1819744 #> 7   2        b       v2  0.8917676 #> 8   3        c       v2  1.3292082 #> 9   4        d       v2 -0.1034661 #> 10  5        e       v2  0.6150646   ##
